q-108830.name: Question 1
q-108830.problem:
Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(2,0)$ and $(0,2),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dx+({x}^{3}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
q-108830.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/2bec8a0243d2ea9e983cab4c07719ff4a5d309960039ccdd77e621fd15ffd7ed.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}y+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dx+({x}^{3}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$

a

b

c
 x3−xy2−cos⁡y
d
x2y
e
 −x2y
Submit

EXPLANATION

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=x2y2 and Q(x,y)=x3y+y. Therefore, ∂P∂y=2x2y,∂Q∂x=3x2y.

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get ∮Cx2y2dx+(x3y+sin⁡y)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(3x2y−2x2y)dA=∬Dx2ydA

q-109129.name: Question 2
q-109129.problem:
Consider the path $C,$ in the plane, as the boundary of the region enclosed by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the $x$-axis, for $y\ge 0,$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}x{e}^{-{y}^{2}}\,dx+{x}^{2}y{e}^{-{y}^{2}}\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
q-109129.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/a0d50e8f2faf679e6dee1471c8fa1ca2be4194796e606fc3e89372f0fefe8cfc.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x{e}^{-{y}^{2}}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y{e}^{-{y}^{2}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{e}^{-{y}^{2}}\,dx+{x}^{2}y{e}^{-{y}^{2}}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}}-(-2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}})]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}}+2xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=4xy{e}^{-{y}^{2}}.$

q-109196.name: Question 3
q-109196.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,1),(0,-1),(1,-1)$ and $(1,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dx-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
q-109196.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/a3e81cfacc47dfa241a5fea64de84e375a58a6d86ceab82c86303763d5e41fe5.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-1,0),(0,-1)$ and $(1,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem,

q-109199.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/f4bb6636c104cf17bcd4b25037a3490ba30b7c1380b152c33504d9015903bdca.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2xy)$ and $Q(x,y)=2{sin}^{2}⁡xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)=2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2xy)\,dx+2{sin}^{2}⁡(xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)-(-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2xy).$

$$

$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/92b9a6c83dd18a5599bbee71d714b26fddd62eb32917a5df983edc232664067b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}},\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x{y}^{2}-{e}^{x})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the closed curve C, which is the boundary of the region enclosed by the circle x2+y2=1 and the y-axis, for x≥0. Express ∮C(xy2−ex)dx+(2x2y−1)dy as a repeated integral.

a

c

EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing D, then Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=xy2−ex and Q(x,y)=2x2y−1. Therefore, ∂P∂y=2xy,∂Q∂x=4xy.

We can express the region D as a type II region as follows: D={(x,y):0≤x≤1−y2,−1≤y≤1}

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get ∮C(xy2−ex)dx+(2x2y−1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(4xy−2xy)dA=∬D2xydA=∫−11∫01−y22xydxdy.

q-42074.name: Question 7
q-42074.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=1-{x}^{2}$ and $y=0.$ Express ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,dx+(2x-{y}^{2})\,dy$ as a repeated integral.
q-42074.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/a3fe0bbc283a2eaacffad4b6be071f601781b6b77b2df0dd9b30abb22653c738.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x-{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,dx+(2x-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-42085.problem: Consider the square $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,3)$ and $(-1,3),$ traversed counterclockwise, and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$  where $F(x,y)=⟨3xy,{x}^{2}y⟩,$ as a repeated integral.
q-42085.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/6f831b2b707e63e8eb34ff5f6c1c45d0267f51001de2560834d212506b48ee41.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}3xy\,dx+{x}^{2}y\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=3xy$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}3xy\,dx+{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-3x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}x(2y-3)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

q-109288.name: Question 9
q-109288.problem: Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0)$ and $(-1,2),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express ${∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-2xy)\,dx+(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2})\,dy$ as a repeated integral.
q-109288.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/eac7a442f0a794db0606b95aa722320d099f2bcc4e530fc6b62e9be889335da2.png)

 

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-2xy$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y-2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-2xy)\,dx+(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[\operatorname{sin}⁡y-2x-(2y-2x)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y-2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

q-109245.name: Question 10
q-109245.problem: Consider the rectangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-2,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ and $(-2,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express ${∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x{y}^{2})\,dy$ as a repeated integral.
q-109245.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/a5404053d83188af931c19350d5b6e42145009cf7f67b9dffcc08edc16ad3627.png)

 

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-2\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

q-41475.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨6{x}^{2}-xy+11,{y}^{2}+1⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,-1)$ and $(2,1).$
q-41475.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/007634ca34871f05cde9d44a58fcf24b1e5fd3b8c337c68f2025fb8724eef819.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(6{x}^{2}-xy+11)\,dx+({y}^{2}+1)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=6{x}^{2}-xy+11$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,-\frac{x}{2}\le y\le \frac{x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(6{x}^{2}-xy+11)\,dx+({y}^{2}+1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[0-(-x)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-x/2}^{x/2}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x[y]_{-x/2}^{x/2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x(x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-109149.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}xy\,dx+(2{x}^{2}+y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is the boundary of the rectangle with vertices at $(-1,0),$ $(3,0),$ $(3,2)$ and $(-1,2).$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/3954846460076fa1ef1e5826d32bde9145e7350cb2324072b001d8c6ff41cc14.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}xy\,dx+(2{x}^{2}+y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4x-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}3x[y]_{0}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}3x(2)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}6x\,dx \\  & =3[{x}^{2}]_{-1}^{3} \\  & =3[9-1] \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

q-41810.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡y,{x}^{2}-2y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the square $0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi ,$ traversed counterclockwise.
q-41810.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120089/assets/4f75ee554c61dc799273c2c731d608766d27987937d0058df6ee1e0290d8b060.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi }
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{[2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi }\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\pi x+2)\,dx \\  & ={[\pi {x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & ={\pi }^{3}+2\pi  \\  & =\pi ({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$
